en: Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the "thorn" (śalya) as they have been described—situated in the center of the site for the purpose of harming living beings. (1)

On a field made square and marked with lines by means of omens and other methods, one who knows the divisions of the body of the site (vāstu) should determine the structural layout (vāstu-śalya). ||2||
When beginning the construction of a house or a palace, a wise man should properly observe the omens and carefully examine the signs during the work of laying the foundation lines.
I carefully observe the appearance, the speech, the voice, and the movements of the sacrificer within his physical body, as they truly are, like a thorn [to be extracted]. (4)
The views of heretics are not desired for householders, as they bring unhappiness;
having heard that [a relative] has been struck down, wounded, killed, or broken, one should not construct a house. ||5||
One should avoid seeing, mentioning, or even hearing the sound of those beings who are unwholesome, undesirable, and censured.
It is necessarily determined that there exists gold of that same measure.

If it is a young girl, then beneath it there will certainly be silver of that same measure. Fear arises; it does not lead to well-being. There is no attainment of wealth. Upon seeing smoke, there is mental anguish. Upon seeing people afflicted by new diseases, there is illness. Auspiciousness occurs upon seeing a lotus, curd, Indra, a flame of fire, fruit, a pair of fish, a king, a woman, and so forth. Upon seeing learned men, Brahmins, mendicants, and virtuous people, there will be righteousness (*dharma*). By the breaking of a thread, death or suffering ending in death occurs.
Having understood this, one who knows the ritual procedure should perform the pacifying oblation.
Since a house that is well-constructed brings all happiness and is endowed with equal prosperity, one should therefore examine for any structural flaw (śalya) after it has been properly built. ||8||
Whether by transgressing the Sūtra, or by seeing it, or by reciting its name, or even by hearing its sound, I shall carefully detect the thorn. (9)
One should diagnose that thorn of a living being by means of fasting and other such methods, based on its appearance, crying, and the naming of its name. ||10||
One should know that the limb of one living being [is the source of harm] because of the leaping over another;
or, by means of a deformity of the limbs of a householder, one should indicate the presence of a structural flaw (śalya) in the building site.
If a bird is seen, or if its cry is heard, or if its name is uttered, one should point out that as the source of the pain. 12.
But while the thread is being stretched out, if the cat should perceive the donkey's bone beneath the site, it should be known that [the house] will fall upon his body. (18)
If a dog leaps over the thread, one should predict the bone of a dog; by the very act of a mouse leaping over it, one should predict the bone of a goat or sheep. ||19||
If there are goats and sheep, it would be a herd of cattle; one should indicate the bones of cows and horses.
By the very leaping of a horse, one should indicate a bovine splinter.
By the very leaping over a buffalo, there would be the bone of a jackal;
by the very leaping over a jackal, one should predict the bone of a boar. ||21||
A tiger [is overcome] by the trampling of a boar; an elephant by a tiger; a camel by the trampling of an elephant; and [a snake] from the leaping over of a woman. ||22||
A human bone [is indicated] by leaping over humans, and a donkey bone by leaping over donkeys;
thus one should identify the foreign body through methods such as leaping and visual inspection. (23)
Silver may be produced from cow urine, and gold indeed from cow dung; iron from cat urine, and lead one should indicate from cat dung. ||32||
If a bird cries sweetly in a peaceful direction, one should understand that there is success in that matter. ||34||
But when there is an itch in the head, one should extract the thorn from the head.
A bone splinter should be known to remain in the mouth for half a man's height [of time] when it causes itching; or it may be caused by a piece of wood or originate from the head. //64//
It remains below at a distance of exactly two cubits; of this there is no doubt.
By touching the teeth with the jaw, one should extract it according to that measure. ||65||
Indeed, one should indicate that the arrowhead is located in whichever limb it touches;
if the neck itches, they know the arrowhead is made of iron chain.
She should be known as Śṛṅkhalā by means of three hands; of this there is no doubt.
When there is itching in a limb, one should diagnose it as a "dart born of the body" (affecting the vital organs). ||67||
One should carefully extract the splinter from below at that same measurement;
however, if the swelling is touched, one should diagnose the splinter as being located in the head of the arrow. ||68||
But when it remains at its proper measure, one should extract it after having correctly understood this;
for when there is an itching in the arm, the bracelet remains on the arm. ||69||
It stands at three and a half cubits; there is no doubt about this.
When there is itching in the hand, one should point to the foot of the bed. (70)
One should know it to be situated at the height of the knees by touching with the fingers and nails; or, when scratching the hand, they know it to be situated at the height of the waist. ||71||
A wise man should extract a splinter, or even a shard of pottery, when there is itching in the chest; likewise, he should extract a splinter from an animal or one originating from his own body. (72)
One should carefully extract the arrow from two and a half cubits below, by touching the heart with the heart; it is of that same measure and composed of that same substance. (73)

One should know that an arrow-head arising from the back is indicated by contact with the back; one arising from the abdomen by its measurement; and one arising from the sides by contact with the sides, as well as those produced from [buried] dust. (74)
The best of those skilled in extracting foreign bodies should extract a shaft lodged in its exact measure by means of contact with the waist, or likewise an iron thorn produced in the waist.
If there is an itching of the thighs or a pain in the thigh that is as severe as if one were struck by a tree, one should extract the foreign object from that spot, which measures two cubits.
One should carefully extract the splinter with a probe measuring one and a half cubits, having observed whether it originated from a thorn or from the knee, as the patient scratches his knee. //77//
When it is raised to the measure of one cubit and the shank is touched, one should indicate that the bone of the shank is there. ||78||
If there is itching in the foot, one should diagnose a boar's tusk as the shaft; it remains eleven finger-breadths below, of this there is no doubt. (79)
When the measure is twelve finger-breadths, one should extract the thorn-like splinter;
when it is at the thumb, one should indicate itching as the chalk-splinter.
One should indicate there iron mixed with brass or painted designs; if one scratches the finger, one should predict an elephant's foot [injury]. ||81||
It remains at a distance of one and a half spans; there is no doubt in this matter.
Having scratched with the little finger, one should indicate the bronze vessel there. ||82||
And that remains at a measurement of eight finger-breadths; there is no doubt about this. One should diagnose the presence of a splinter beneath the skin by means of itching. 83.
"A thorn-like splinter remains at a depth of eight finger-breadths"— thus ends the chapter on the extraction of foreign bodies; indeed,
a thorn-like splinter remains at a depth of eight finger-breadths.
Thus ends the chapter on the extraction of the arrow in the *Śitā*.
